title_en: Hu Jinqing and Wu Yunchu v. Shanghai Animation Film Studio — dispute over copyright ownership
ruling_gist_en: A work created by a citizen to complete a work task assigned by a legal person is a service work. However, in the mid-1980s, before China's Copyright Law was enacted, when an employee created character design artwork in the course of his duties for the unit's need to produce an animated film, the ownership of the creative output should be determined based on a comprehensive analysis of the contemporary background, historical conditions, and the conduct of both parties at the time of creation. The nature of the work should be determined as a special service work, with the author only enjoying the right of attribution, while the other copyright rights are enjoyed by the legal person. The so-called historical background includes the economic system, legal system, social reality, and generally accepted common understanding; the conduct of the parties can be explored in depth from aspects such as the unit's rules and regulations, express prohibitions, receipt of remuneration, and the words and actions of both parties.

full_text_en:
**Hu Jinqing and Wu Yunchu v. Shanghai Animation Film Studio — dispute over ownership of copyright**

**[Ruling Summary]**

A work created by a citizen to fulfill a work task assigned by a legal person constitutes a work made for hire. However, in the mid-1980s, prior to the enactment of the Copyright Law of the People's Republic of China, where an employee, in order to meet the needs of the employer's animation film production, created a character design artwork within the scope of his or her duties, the ownership of such creative output shall be determined by a comprehensive analysis of the historical background of the time, the circumstances of the era, and the conduct of both parties. Such works shall be characterized as special works made for hire, whereby the author is entitled only to the right of attribution, while all other copyright rights are vested in the legal person. The so-called historical background includes the economic system, legal framework, social realities, and generally accepted common understandings; the conduct of the parties may be examined in depth through the employer's internal regulations, express prohibitions, the remuneration received, and the words and actions of both parties.

**Plaintiffs:** Hu Jinqing, male, born April 15, 1936, Han Chinese, residing at Wanchun Street, Jing'an District, Shanghai.

**Plaintiff:** Wu Yunchu, male, born December 13, 1941, Han Chinese, residing at Wuding West Road, Jing'an District, Shanghai.

**Defendant:** Shanghai Animation Film Studio, domiciled at Wanhangdu Road, Jing'an District, Shanghai.

**Legal Representative:** Wang Tianyun, Vice President of Shanghai Film (Group) Co., Ltd.

Plaintiffs Hu Jinqing and Wu Yunchu filed this lawsuit with the Huangpu District People's Court of Shanghai against the Defendant, Shanghai Animation Film Studio (hereinafter referred to as the "Animation Studio"), regarding a dispute over ownership of copyright.

**The two plaintiffs alleged:**

1. As early as 1984, before the establishment of the "Calabash Brothers" production crew, Plaintiff Hu Jinqing began creating the "Calabash Boy" character design artwork and contemplating the Animation Studio's first series of paper-cut animation films. Unlike modern animated films, paper-cut animation at that time required the director to draw storyboards integrating plot, text, character design, and shooting methods using ink brushes. In March 1984 and May 1984, Plaintiff Hu Jinqing drew the storyboards for Episode 3 and Episodes 1 and 2 of *Calabash Brothers*, respectively, sketching the basic artistic form containing the characteristics of the "Calabash Boy" including hairstyle, face shape, body type, clothing, and neck ornament, establishing the principle of distinguishing the seven brothers by seven colors. Plaintiff Wu Yunchu enhanced the calabash crown ornament, changing Hu Jinqing's original design of a diamond-shaped headdress hinting at a calabash shape with a leaf on the right side, into a calabash crown on the head with a leaf embellishment on each side, and drew the front view perfected draft, side view draft, and color draft of the "Calabash Boy" artistic design. This design was fully adopted by the Defendant at the end of 1985 after a studio-wide solicitation and selection, and was used in the films. Therefore, the two plaintiffs are the original creators of the "Calabash Boy" character design image. From March to October 1986, Plaintiff Hu Jinqing drew the storyboards for Episodes 4 to 13 of *Calabash Brothers*, which were assigned to two production crews for filming.

2. From January to June 1988, Plaintiff Hu Jinqing drew the storyboards for six episodes of *Calabash Little King Kong*, the sequel to *Calabash Brothers*. The design of the "King Kong Calabash Boy" was essentially identical to the "Calabash Boy," except that he was dressed in white clothes and wore a sparkling golden calabash pendant on his neck. In the credits at the end of each episode of the two films, it stated "Character Design: Jinqing, Wu Yunchu," indicating that the Defendant acknowledged the two plaintiffs as the creators of the "Calabash Boy" character design.

3. The two plaintiffs never used the Defendant's material and technical resources to create the storyboards for the films in question, and there was no agreement between the plaintiffs and the Defendant regarding the copyright in the character design artwork. The Defendant's alleged act of organizing the film's principal creators to immerse themselves in real life had no relevance to the creation of the "Calabash Boy" character design artwork. The plaintiffs have received the remuneration and distribution of award bonuses for the films in question, but such amounts constitute labor fees and are unrelated to the copyright in the artwork in question. Although the final version of the "Calabash Boy" character design artwork was decided by the Defendant, its creation was initiated by the two plaintiffs on their own accord, and thus it should be considered a work made for hire, not a legal person work.

4. Although the "Calabash Boy" character design artwork was created before the effective date of the Copyright Law, since the work in question remains within the term of protection, the Copyright Law may be applied retroactively to the dispute in this case. In art films, the vehicle for character performance is a virtual image created by an artwork made by a person; the character design artwork exists before the film itself. According to the provisions of the Copyright Law, the copyright in this artwork, which can be independent of the film, should be vested in the authors, i.e., the two plaintiffs. Moreover, the copyright in the "Calabash Boy" image reflected in the films should also belong to the two plaintiffs. Therefore, the plaintiffs request the court to confirm that the copyright in the original character design artwork of the "Calabash Boy" (i.e., the Calabash Brothers and the King Kong Calabash Boy) in the series of paper-cut animation films *Calabash Brothers* and its sequel *Calabash Little King Kong* belongs to Plaintiffs Hu Jinqing and Wu Yunchu.

**The Defendant Animation Studio argued in defense:**

1. The character design in dispute was drawn in drafts by the two plaintiffs and others, posted within the production crew, discussed and revised collectively by crew members, and repeatedly discussed and improved by the Animation Studio's Creative Office and Art Committee, with the final version approved by the Animation Studio's Art Committee. Plaintiff Hu Jinqing drew the storyboards based on the finalized script, character design, and background design, which was part of his duties as director. The Defendant does not deny the contributions of the two plaintiffs to the character design in dispute. However, the creation of the work was carried out under the leadership of the Defendant, reflecting the legal person's will, and the legal person bears responsibility; thus, it is a legal person work. The credit given to the two plaintiffs was because, at the time the production crew was established, their assigned positions were responsible for character design, and the two plaintiffs executed the actual drawing.

2. The production of the films in question took place against the backdrop of a planned economy. The Defendant prepared filming plans based on production task indicators assigned by the state, reported them to the Film Bureau for approval, and then established production crews for filming. All production personnel were assigned by the Defendant, work tasks were allocated by the Defendant, and after completion, the films were uniformly purchased and distributed by the state according to plan. All expenses for the film's principal creators to immerse themselves in real life, investment in filming, production, publishing, and distribution were borne by the Defendant. Since the Copyright Law had not yet been enacted at that time, it was impossible for the parties to enter into a contract stipulating the ownership of copyright.

3. According to the Defendant's regulations, each director was required to complete one feature-length film (approximately 20 minutes) or two short films (approximately 10 minutes) per year; other creators followed the director's standards to complete corresponding work. Starting with the *Calabash Brothers* film, a remuneration system was implemented for creators for the first time. *Calabash Brothers* also won multiple domestic and international awards, and the bonuses were distributed proportionally to the principal creators.

4. The creation of the "Calabash Boy" character design was for the purpose of filming. The image of the Calabash Boy in the films is continuous and dynamic; extracting any single frame for separate use lacks legal basis. The character design cannot be used separately from the film. Even if it could be used separately, the copyright should be vested in the Defendant, as this would be more conducive to the development of the animation industry. In conclusion, the Defendant requests the court to dismiss the plaintiffs' claims.

**The Huangpu District People's Court of Shanghai found the following facts upon first-instance trial:**

**I. The plaintiffs' employment history at the Defendant**

Plaintiff Hu Jinqing, also known as Mo Du and Jinqing, started working at the Defendant Animation Studio in 1953, successively serving as animation designer, motion designer, character designer, director, and deputy director of the Art Committee. Plaintiff Wu Yunchu started working at the Defendant in August 1964, successively serving as motion designer, character designer, animation supervisor, and director. In March 1988 and October 1996, Plaintiffs Hu Jinqing and Wu Yunchu were promoted to first-level director and first-level art designer, respectively.

**II. Background of the creation of the films in question**

On November 9, 1985, the Defendant Animation Studio submitted its 1986 thematic plan to the Film Bureau of the Ministry of Culture, listing a total of 40 reels of various films under the tentative program, including eight reels of the paper-cut film *Seven Brothers* (folklore). On March 3, 1986, Shanghai Film Corporation issued a document titled "Arrangement of Various Task Indicators for 1986" to its subordinate units and departments, setting targets including production, copy printing, distribution and screening, profit plans, and labor personnel, and clarifying an improved bonus distribution method, discontinuing position (duty) allowances as of January 1, and implementing a remuneration system for creators. On January 12, 1987, Shanghai Film Corporation reported to the Shanghai Municipal People's Government in its "Overview of the 1986 Work of Shanghai Film Corporation," stating that under the leadership of the Ministry of Radio, Film and Television, the Shanghai Municipal Party Committee, the Municipal Government, and the Municipal Party Committee Propaganda Department, major indicators such as creative production, copy printing, and distribution revenue had exceeded the annual plan. The main breakthrough in art film production this year was the attempt to create series films, including the paper-cut film *Calabash Brothers*, among five series films, which received varying degrees of positive feedback after previews and satisfied the social demand for domestic series art films.

Witnesses Shen Rudong (then motion designer for the films in question), Gong Jinfu (then motion designer and scenery painter for the films in question), and Shen Shoulin (then motion designer for the films in question) all testified: Storyboards serve as the outline or guide for filming. During filming, a paper-cut version of the finalized character design had to be made first, and motion designers animated the character design. For special expressions, special actions, profiles, or back views, the motion designers had to design based on the finalized character design, then hand it over to the drawing team for production, after which the scenery painter drew the background. Finally, the motion designers manipulated the moving character designs to shoot continuous frames based on the principle of 24 frames per second. Around 1986, directors and other creators were required to fulfill the annual task indicators assigned by the Defendant's Creative Office. Each director had to complete one feature-length film (approximately 20 minutes) or two short films (approximately 10 minutes) per year, primarily assigned by the Defendant; other creators followed the director to complete corresponding workloads, and all creative output belonged to the unit. The Defendant also regularly organized creators to immerse themselves in real life or provided job-related training. Starting with the *Calabash Brothers* film, the Defendant abolished the monthly bonus of RMB 5 and implemented a remuneration system for creators. With respect to the films in question, witnesses Shen Rudong and Shen Shoulin confirmed that, in addition to salaries and benefits, they all received corresponding remuneration and distribution of award bonuses after the films were completed.

**III. Creation of the "Calabash Boy" design and the films**

In 1984, Yang Yuliang of the Defendant Animation Studio's Literature Department created a literary script outline for *Seven Brothers* based on the folklore *Seven Brothers*. At the end of 1985, the Defendant established the production crew for the film *Seven Brothers*, assigning Hu Jinqing, Zhou Keqin, and Ge Guiyun as directors, and Hu Jinqing and Wu Yunchu as character designers. The two plaintiffs drew the "Calabash Boy" character design drafts. The designs of the seven Calabash Brothers were identical, with the following common features: square faces, short thick eyebrows, bright large eyes, sturdy bodies, calabash crowns on their heads, calabash leaf necklaces around their necks, sleeveless shirts and shorts, and calabash leaf aprons around their waists. The colors of the seven brothers' clothing were red, orange, yellow, green, cyan, blue, and purple, respectively. Plaintiff Hu Jinqing successively drew storyboards for all 13 episodes of *Calabash Brothers*. To speed up production, from January to December 1986, the Defendant established two production crews for odd-numbered and even-numbered episodes. Upon comparison, the "Calabash Boy" character design in the storyboards was essentially identical in appearance to the "Calabash Boy" in the films. The former was black-and-white, roughly drawn, and inconsistent in details throughout. The latter was colored, finely crafted, and consistent throughout, and when combined with plot, dialogue, dubbing, and scenes, it exhibited personality traits such as righteousness, kindness, intelligence, courage, unity, and cooperation. In 1988, Plaintiff Hu Jinqing successively drew storyboards for all six episodes of *Calabash Little King Kong*. The design of the "King Kong Calabash Boy" was essentially identical to that of the "Calabash Boy," except that he was dressed in white clothes and wore a sparkling golden calabash pendant on his neck, indicating that the "King Kong Calabash Boy" was formed by the combination of the seven Calabash Brothers.

**IV. Credits on the films in question**

The film catalog compiled and printed by the Film Administration Bureau of the Ministry of Radio, Film and Television of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter referred to as the "Film Bureau of the Ministry of Radio, Film and Television") showed that the art design credits for each episode of *Calabash Brothers* and *Calabash Little King Kong* were generally attributed to Wu Yunchu, Jinqing, and Chang Baosheng. The completion scripts for each episode of *Calabash Brothers* and the VCD disc set of the *Calabash Brothers* series produced by the Defendant in 1996 listed the following staff credits at the end of each episode: For odd-numbered episodes, the creators included: Screenwriters: Yao Zhongli, Yang Yuliang, Mo Du; Directors: Hu Jinqing, Ge Guiyun; Character Design: Wu Yunchu, Jinqing; Background Design: Chang Baosheng; Motion Design: Xiao Gang and 4 others; Scenery Painting: Ge Zhan and 2 others; Drawing: Yue Huimin and 3 others — involving a total of 21 job categories, 34 staff members, and groups such as the Shanghai Film Orchestra and the Chorus of the Shanghai Children's Palace. For even-numbered episodes, the creators included: Directors: Hu Jinqing, Zhou Keqin; Motion Design: Shen Zuwei and 5 others; Scenery Painting: Shen Tongchun and 5 others; Drawing: Yue Huimin and 1 other; the rest was essentially the same as for odd-numbered episodes, involving a total of 21 job categories, 36 staff members, and two groups. The completion scripts for each episode of *Calabash Little King Kong* listed: Screenwriters: Yao Zhongli, Mo Du; Character Design: Wu Yunchu, Jinqing; General Director: Hu Jinqing.

**V. Distribution and screening of the films in question**

According to the film catalogs compiled and printed by the Film Bureau of the Ministry of Radio, Film and Television in March 1987 and March 1988, respectively, for the years 1986 and 1987: Episodes 1 to 9 of *Calabash Brothers* were completed in 1986, and Episodes 10 to 13 were completed in 1987. According to the film catalogs compiled and printed by the Film Administration Bureau of the Ministry of Radio, Film and Television in March 1990, March 1991, and March 1992, respectively, for the years 1989, 1990, and 1991: Episodes 1 to 3 of *Calabash Little King Kong* were completed in 1989, Episodes 4 to 5 were completed in 1990, and Episode 6 was completed in 1991. The films in question were initially broadcast on television as paper-cut animation films and later released in cinemas. In 1996, the Defendant Animation Studio produced and published the two films in question as a set of six VCDs. The packaging showed: Produced by Shanghai Animation Film Studio; Published and distributed by Shanghai Film Audio & Video Publishing House; China Standard Audiovisual Product Code: ISRC CN-E28-96-0062-0/V.J9. In 2008, the Defendant compiled the 13 episodes of *Calabash Brothers* into one film for public screening. All expenses for investment in filming, copy printing, publishing and distribution, broadcasting on television and in cinemas, and distribution in the audio-visual market were borne by the Defendant.

**VI. Distribution of awards for the films in question**

On August 18, 1986, the Film Bureau of the Ministry of Radio, Film and Television sent a letter to various film studios including the Defendant Animation Studio regarding the distribution of bonuses for outstanding films of 1985, stating: "We are now distributing the bonuses awarded by the Ministry of Radio, Film and Television to various types of outstanding films. The distribution of bonuses shall still be handled according to our Bureau's regulations, i.e., the full amount of the bonus shall be given to the production crew of the award-winning film, with 60% to be distributed to the principal creators. To encourage directors to produce more outstanding films, the amount of the bonus allocated to directors shall be appropriately increased starting this year." On January 15, 1988, the Defendant's Creative Office recommended four films, including the paper-cut film *Calabash Brothers* (Episodes 3 and 4), to the Film Bureau of the Ministry of Radio, Film and Television for selection as outstanding films of 1986. On May 20, 1988, the Defendant submitted to the Film Bureau a list of participants for the 1986 and 1987 Outstanding Film Awards Ceremony, which included representatives for the *Calabash Brothers* film: Director Hu Jinqing and Motion Designer Shen Rudong. On the same day, the Defendant sent a letter to the Film Bureau stating that *Calabash Brothers*, one of the outstanding art films selected, was a series of paper-cut films (13 episodes) produced in 1986 and 1987. When submitting for selection, the studio had only selected Episodes 3 and 4 for the judges to review. To encourage the creation of future series art films, the studio hoped that the Bureau, when considering the bonus for *Calabash Brothers*, would give appropriate preferential treatment in accordance with the standards for series feature-length films. On August 19, 1988, the Defendant distributed a bonus of RMB 7,000 for the 1986 Outstanding Film Award to the creators of *Calabash Brothers*. In addition, *Calabash Brothers* also won the 1987 Children's Film "Tong Niu Award."

**The issues in dispute at first instance were:**

1. Whether the "Calabash Boy" character design constitutes a work and who created it;
2. The nature of the "Calabash Boy" character design artwork as a work;
3. Whether the "Calabash Boy" character design can be used as a work capable of separate use and whether the author may independently exercise copyright therein;
4. The relationship between the "Calabash Boy" image and the "Calabash Boy" character design artwork.

**The Huangpu District People's Court of Shanghai held at first instance:**

**I. Whether the "Calabash Boy" character design constitutes a work and who created it**

Whether it is the literary folk tale *Seven Brothers* in classical Chinese, the widely circulated story of ten brothers, or the literary script outline for *Seven Brothers* for the film in question, all are literary works. Even the script of *Calabash Brothers* and the descriptions of the "Calabash Boy" therein constitute a form of literary expression. The author of the "Calabash Boy" character design was the first to delineate the basic form of the "Calabash Boy" using lines. The square face reflects kindness and integrity; the short thick eyebrows, long eyelashes, bright large eyes, and small mouth with red lips reveal the child's innocence and cleverness; the strong and powerful lines of the hands and legs imply boundless strength and ability; the matching of the upper sleeveless shirt with the lower shorts appears capable and neat; the calabash crown ornament on the head, set off by two tender leaves, the black collar adorned with two calabash tender leaves, and the calabash leaf apron around the waist clearly showing the veins of the leaves, are both layered and echo each other. It skillfully combines the calabash with the image of a Chinese boy, creating the "Calabash Boy" character design that is bright-eyed, vigorous, innocent, and adorable, and distinguishes the seven brothers by seven colors, indicating their brotherhood while also differentiating them. This reflects the author's ingenuity and painting skills. The visual image formed by hand-drawing, combined with lines, contours, clothing, and color, creates a specific and fixed "Calabash Boy" character design that no longer remains at the level of abstract concepts or ideas. Its aesthetic significance, artistry, originality, and reproducibility meet the constituent elements of a work under the Copyright Law of the People's Republic of China and should be protected by the Copyright Law. As for the "King Kong Calabash Boy," since it is essentially identical to the basic design of the "Calabash Boy," with only minor modifications to the color of the clothes and the neck ornament, it does not constitute a new work and can be subsumed under a single "Calabash Boy" character design. Therefore, the court finds that the "Calabash Boy" character design constitutes a work of fine art.

### Translation of Part 2/3

**Regarding the question of who created the "Gourd Boys" character design**, the two plaintiffs neither provided a finalized artistic work of the "Gourd Boys" character design nor had they ever registered the copyright for such work. The 70-page storyboard provided by Plaintiff Hu Jinqing to prove his authorship was incomplete, lacked both the author's signature and the date of creation. The episode titles were added afterwards or bore signs of alteration, and storyboards are not equivalent to character designs. The three pieces of "Gourd Boys" design artwork provided by Plaintiff Hu Jinqing had no date of creation or author's signature. The 6 pages of character art materials for "Calabash Brothers" and "Calabash Youth" provided by Plaintiff Wu Yunchu also lacked dates and signatures, were clearly created after the completion of the "Calabash Brothers" film, i.e., produced post factum, and moreover, these design drafts still differed from the "Gourd Boys" image in the film. The witnesses presented by the plaintiffs did not appear in court to testify. Therefore, this court does not admit the aforementioned evidence. Consequently, the evidence provided by the two plaintiffs is insufficient to prove that they independently created the artistic work of the "Gourd Boys" character design. However, the film catalog of the case, the completed scripts for each episode, and the staff credits at the end of each episode of the "Calabash Brothers" series VCD released by the studio in 1996 all indicate: Character Design: Wu Yunchu, Jinqing. Both parties have had no objection to this attribution since the completion of the film. Defendant Shanghai Animation Film Studio also acknowledges the contribution of the two plaintiffs to the design at issue. Pursuant to the provision of我国的 Copyright Law that, in the absence of contrary proof, the citizen, legal person, or other organization named as the author on a work shall be deemed the author, the court determines that the two plaintiffs jointly created the artistic work of the "Gourd Boys" character design.

### II. Nature of the "Gourd Boys" Design Artistic Work

Legal systems typically reflect a country's economic, cultural, social, and temporal characteristics. The determination of ownership in this case cannot be divorced from the era in which the work was created and the legal framework of that time. First, from a macro social reality perspective, a series of evidence provided by Defendant Studio shows that during the creation of the film in question, China was in the planned economy period. As a wholly state-owned entity, the creation of the film had to strictly follow administrative approval procedures, and the distribution and screening of the film had to strictly comply with national plans. For example, annual creative themes and plans had to be submitted based on targets issued by higher authorities; personnel arrangements were made according to the beginning-of-year plan; creative outcomes belonged to the unit; the unit then handed over the final creative results to relevant entities for unified publication and distribution; and at the end of the year, the completion of various target tasks had to be reported to higher authorities and government departments. At the time of creation, the two plaintiffs, as design personnel of the defendant, completing the work tasks assigned by the defendant was precisely their duty. The creative results belonging to the unit was an undisputed industry practice and a generally accepted societal norm. Second, from the perspective of the legal system at that time, the "General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China," effective January 1, 1987, only provided in principle in Article 94 that citizens and legal persons enjoy copyright, including the rights to attribution, publication, publication, and remuneration. It did not stipulate the ownership of copyright in cinematographic works nor which works within a cinematographic work could be used independently with the author exercising copyright independently. Referable is the "Trial Regulations on Copyright Protection for Books and Periodicals," effective January 1, 1985, and now expired, which only stipulated that copyright of works published in the name of organs, organizations, enterprises, or institutions, or other collective names, belongs to the unit or collective. At the time of creation of the work in dispute, it was impossible for the parties to have expressly agreed in advance by contract on the ownership of copyright in works made for hire, as stipulated by the Copyright Law of our country, which came into effect on June 1, 1991. Therefore, there is no legal basis for determining that the two plaintiffs enjoyed property rights in the copyright of their work at the time of its creation. Third, from a micro perspective of internal rules and regulations, the testimonies of three witnesses provided by the defendant all confirm that during the creation of the film, the director and other staff were required to complete annual task targets set by the Studio's Creation Office, and other creative personnel followed the director to complete corresponding workloads. Both the plaintiff and the defendant acknowledge that the defendant established a production team for the film, appointed Plaintiff Hu Jinqing as director, and the two plaintiffs as character designers. This constituted completing work tasks assigned by the defendant. It is evident that completing task targets assigned by the legal person, receiving wages, bonuses, and related welfare benefits such as medical care and housing allocation, while the creative outcomes belong to the legal person, was in line with the common understanding of people in that society and was a generally accepted code of conduct for the public. Fourth, regarding rewards received, a document issued by the defendant's superior company in March 1986 explicitly stipulated that, effective January 1, creative personnel would adopt a fee system. On August 18, 1986, the Film Bureau of the Ministry of Radio, Film and Television issued a letter clearly stating: bonuses would be awarded in full to the production team of the award-winning film, with 60% distributed to the main creative personnel; to encourage directors to produce more excellent films, starting from that year, the bonuses allocated to directors should be appropriately increased. The system design itself indicates that under the historical conditions of the time, the state encouraged, respected, and reflected the creative value of the main creative personnel of the film. The aforementioned documents, combined with the statements of the two plaintiffs, the testimonies of three witnesses regarding receipt of fees and bonuses, and the financial vouchers provided by the defendant, all indicate that for the creation of the work in dispute, the two plaintiffs had already received fees and bonuses far exceeding wages and bonuses. Furthermore, there is no evidence that the two plaintiffs had raised any objections to the defendant regarding this matter from the initial broadcast of the film in 1986 until the date the plaintiffs filed this lawsuit in 2010—a period of 24 years. Moreover, during the 24 years after the work was completed, the two plaintiffs never objected to the defendant regarding the copyright of the disputed design. In summary, based on the historical background and conditions at the time of creation of the work in dispute, and the aforementioned conduct of both parties, it can be determined that the copyright in the artistic work of the "Gourd Boys" character design is owned by the defendant, and the two plaintiffs only have the right to assert their authorship.

As for the defendant's argument that the work in dispute constitutes a legal person work, the court holds that although the two plaintiffs were unit employees, character design was within their job responsibilities, the work was created under the auspices of the unit to fulfill the unit's work tasks, and liability was borne by the unit, we cannot simply equate the will of a legal person with the unit assigning work tasks, raising general requirements for creation, or offering suggestions for revisions or improvements. Otherwise, all works made for hire could be deemed legal person works, and natural persons who are creators would lose their status as authors. The creation of the artistic work in question did not require significant reliance on the unit's material and technical conditions, nor did the creative process reflect the unit's will; rather, it embodied the author's unique thoughts, emotions, will, and personality. The choice of lines, contours, colors, and details such as clothing, neck ornaments, waist ornaments, and gourd crowns for the "Gourd Boys" character design all reflect the author's personal conception, selection, and expression. Although the defendant claims that other members of the production team and department heads of the defendant offered revision suggestions, this does not affect the fact that the substantive contribution to the "Gourd Boys" character design was still made by the individual authors. Moreover, based on the credits at the end of the film, the character design is attributed to the two plaintiffs individually. Therefore, the artistic work of the "Gourd Boys" character design is not a creation representing the will of a legal person and should not be deemed a legal person work. The court does not accept the defendant's assertion on this point.

### III. Whether the "Gourd Boys" Character Design Can Be Used as an Independently Usable Work and Whether the Authors Can Independently Exercise Copyright

The application of Paragraph 2 of Article 15 of the Copyright Law of our country, which states that "authors of scripts, music, and other works that can be used independently in cinematographic works and works created by methods similar to cinematography are entitled to independently exercise their copyright," requires three preconditions: First, the status of author. Its significance lies in further protecting the independent copyright of co-authors in cinematographic works. If one is not the author of the work, one cannot be a qualified subject for the application of this clause and loses the prerequisite for independent protection. In this case, the Defendant Studio attributed character design to the two plaintiffs in the film's credits, which constitutes an acknowledgment that the two plaintiffs are the authors of the artistic work of the film's character design. Second, the property rights in copyright belong to that author. Only when the author has obtained property rights in copyright can the scriptwriter, lyricist, composer, etc., independently exercise their copyright. Conversely, if the property rights in copyright belong to a legal person or other organization, even if one is indeed the author of the work, one has no right to exercise the property rights in copyright of that work, let alone independently exercise its copyright. That is, only when, according to Article 11 and Paragraph 1 of Article 16 of the Copyright Law, the property rights in copyright belong to the author, can this clause be applied. In this case, as previously discussed, the copyright in the work in dispute should belong to the defendant, and the two plaintiffs only enjoy the right to assert authorship. Therefore, the two plaintiffs lose the prerequisite for applying this clause. Third, the work must be capable of independent use. So-called independent use does not mean capturing any single frame from the film for use. A film frame is an inseparable component of the overall expression of the film; it does not have an expression independent of the film itself. It still expresses the characters or storyline within the settings and scenes established by the film. Such use remains use of the film, not independent use of other works within the film. Although this clause only specifically mentions scripts and music, the character design at issue can be extracted from the film and used independently on other goods or service identifiers. In fact, numerous copyright infringement lawsuits filed separately by both the plaintiffs and the defendant over the years also indirectly confirm that the work in dispute has been used independently by others apart from the film. Therefore, the artistic work of the "Gourd Boys" character design qualifies as a work that can be used independently. All three preconditions must be satisfied simultaneously for this clause to apply. Since the two plaintiffs do not enjoy copyright in the work in dispute except for the right of attribution, they cannot invoke this clause to obtain legal protection.

### IV. Relationship Between the "Gourd Boys" Image and the "Gourd Boys" Character Design Artistic Work

During the trial, the two plaintiffs repeatedly asserted that the copyright they claim also covers every "Gourd Boys" image reflected in the film. The court holds that, with respect to each "Gourd Boys" image present in the film, since the two plaintiffs have consented to the Defendant Studio filming their work, and both parties agree that the overall copyright of the cinematographic work should be exercised by the defendant, the court does not accept the plaintiffs' claim that the copyright in the "Gourd Boys" images within the film belongs to them.

After the disputed character design artistic work entered the film, through the creative labor of animators, background designers, artists, cameramen, scriptwriters, directors, voice actors, and others, a complete "Gourd Boys" image with individual characteristics was formed. This image comprises elements such as name, identity, appearance, voice, personality traits, the character's experiences and stories in specific settings, and the character's reactions to people and objects. These constitutive factors of the image constitute a holistic "Gourd Boys" image. When people see a static "Gourd Boys" image, it is no longer simply a piece of artwork but a vivid image encompassing personality traits, plot elements, reactions, and other components. Therefore, the court determines that the Defendant Studio contributed to the overall coherence of the "Gourd Boys" image. Regarding the popularity of the "Gourd Boys" image, considering the evidence provided by the defendant and its submissions, the popularity of the "Gourd Boys" image—to the extent that it became a household name and a beloved animated character for audiences—resulted from: (1) the defendant's decision in 1986 to invest in the production of the "Calabash Brothers" series of paper-cut animated films; (2) the defendant's continuous release of nineteen episodes in the "Calabash Brothers" and "Calabash Youth" series of paper-cut animated films from 1986 to 1991; and (3) over more than two decades, the defendant publicly, widely, continuously, and comprehensively disseminated the film and the "Gourd Boys" image through means such as television broadcasts, cinema screenings, and distribution of VCDs and other media, transforming it into a representation of a lovable Chinese boy with qualities of intelligence, bravery, righteousness, and cooperation, achieving positive public reception among a broad audience of children and even adults, and enjoying considerable popularity in society. The two plaintiffs have never objected to the defendant's investments, publications, distributions, or other related actions. Therefore, from the perspective of the fairness principle in civil law, the contribution to the overall coherence and popularity of the "Gourd Boys" image should be attributed to the defendant. Consequently, the court does not support the plaintiffs' claim that the copyright in the "Gourd Boys" image within the film belongs to them.

In summary, in accordance with Item (4) of Article 3, Paragraphs 1, 2, and 4 of Article 11, Article 15, Item (2) of Paragraph 2 of Article 16, Article 60, and Article 61 of the "Copyright Law of the People's Republic of China," Items (8) and (11) of Article 4 of the "Regulations for the Implementation of the Copyright Law of the People's Republic of China," Paragraph 1 of Article 11 of the said Regulations, and Article 4 of the "General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China," the Shanghai Huangpu District People's Court rendered the following judgment on August 4, 2011:

**Judgment:** The plaintiffs' claim for confirmation that the copyright in the original artistic works of the character design for "Gourd Boys" (i.e., Calabash Brothers and Calabash Youth) in the "Calabash Brothers" and its sequel "Calabash Youth" series of paper-cut animated films belongs to the plaintiffs Hu Jinqing and Wu Yunchu is not supported.

Dissatisfied with the first-instance judgment, Hu Jinqing and Wu Yunchu appealed to the Shanghai Second Intermediate People's Court, requesting the vacatur of the first-instance judgment and a judgment in their favor. Their main reasons were as follows: (1) The "Gourd Boys" image in the storyboards for the first three episodes submitted by the appellants constitutes the original artistic work of the Gourd Brothers and Calabash Youth character images, created by the appellants in 1984. The first-instance court's factual finding on this point was erroneous; (2) The appellants should enjoy complete copyright in the "Gourd Boys" work made for hire, not merely the right of attribution. The first-instance court's application of law was incorrect.

The appellee, Shanghai Animation Film Studio, argued against the appellants' appeal, contending that the storyboards cannot prove that the appellants own the copyright in the "Gourd Boys" design, as they were created after the design was finalized. The appellee maintained its position from the first instance, namely that the "Calabash Brothers" film and the "Gourd Boys" image were created under the collective leadership of the Studio and constitute a legal person work.

During the second instance, the appellants submitted issues of the "Animation King" magazine (Issue 6, 1986; Issue 2, 1987; Issue 3, 1987) to prove that the comic "Calabash Brothers" was serialized in the magazine co-published by the appellee before the animated film was released, with the appellants credited as authors. They argued that this showed that the appellee encouraged and recognized that the copyright in the "Gourd Boys" design belonged to the appellants and that the appellants actually enjoyed economic benefits from the artistic work. The appellee acknowledged the fact that the comic was published before the film's release but argued that this fact does not prove that the appellants own the copyright in the "Gourd Boys" design. Upon the appellants' application, the second-instance court summoned witnesses Yan Dingxian (then president of the Studio) and Jiang Youyi (then director of the Studio's Creation Office) to testify in court. Based on the witness testimonies and related evidence, it was found that, starting in the mid-1980s, the appellee advocated for the creation of series animated films. In 1984, Yang Yuliang created a synopsis for a literary script titled "Seven Brothers," which was approved by the studio. Subsequently, Hu Jinqing independently created several scripts and initial designs for "Calabash Brothers." Wu Yunchu then supplemented and modified the "Gourd Boys" design. It was submitted to the Studio's Creation Office for review, and after approval, submitted to the president for final approval. In November 1985, "Calabash Brothers" (initially named "Seven Brothers") was formally established as a project, a production team was formed, and filming commenced. At that time, the Studio had no regulations regarding the ownership of rights in works. Both the studio and the authors lacked a concept of copyright, and discussing rights issues was considered "a very dishonorable thing." During the filming of "Calabash Brothers," Jiang Youyi explicitly instructed creative personnel not to submit the comic for publication externally during the filming period, but after the film was completed, the studio did not interfere with such submissions.

The Shanghai Second Intermediate People's Court confirmed the other facts found in the first instance through the second-instance trial.

The Shanghai Second Intermediate People's Court held in the second instance that, viewing the creative process of animated films, the character image in an animated film should have a prior static design. If this design constitutes an artistic work, it is entitled to protection under copyright law. In this case, both parties confirmed that the disputed design—the "Gourd Boys" character image—was initially created by Hu Jinqing and subsequently modified by Wu Yunchu. Although the appellee argued that the design was finalized by incorporating collective opinions and representing the appellee's will, based on the available evidence, before the "Calabash Brothers" animated film was formally established as a project, Hu Jinqing had already independently created the initial "Gourd Boys" design. It was supplemented and modified by Wu Yunchu, and then submitted to the relevant department of the Studio for review. Although the final "Gourd Boys" design underwent certain modifications by other creative personnel at the Studio, these modifications did not result in a substantial difference from the original, nor did they constitute a new work. Therefore, it is difficult to prove that the "Gourd Boys" design was created under the auspices of the appellee and represents its will. Furthermore, although the "Seven Brothers" literary script synopsis existed at the time, its content differed significantly from the later "Calabash Brothers." Moreover, the character design did not yet exist at that time. Hence, it cannot be concluded that the "Gourd Boys" design was derived from "Seven Brothers." In summary, the court confirmed that the disputed "Gourd Boys" design artistic work does not fall under the circumstance specified in Paragraph 3 of Article 11 of the Copyright Law, i.e., it is not a "legal person work."

On the other hand, the appellants submitted the storyboards for the first three episodes of "Calabash Brothers" as evidence of the original artistic work of the "Gourd Boys" design. The first-instance court did not admit this storyboard due to its lack of formal requirements, and the second-instance court expresses no disagreement with that decision. However, proving the ownership of copyright in a work is not necessarily linked to the work's physical medium. In other words, even if the appellants failed to submit the original of the claimed design work, this does not mean their rights should be denied. In this case, based on the credits in the "Calabash Brothers" animated film, witness testimonies, and the parties' descriptions of the creative process, it is sufficient to confirm that the appellants created the disputed "Gourd Boys" character design artistic work and that it was created to fulfill the unit's work tasks. Therefore, the work in dispute falls under the category of works made for hire as defined in Article 16 of the Copyright Law. The key issue in this case is the ownership of copyright in this work made for hire.

The disputed design artistic work was created before the Copyright Law came into effect. The laws, regulations, and policies at that time did not provide for the ownership of copyright in works made for hire. Since the work in question is still within the term of copyright protection, this case should be handled by applying the current provisions of the Copyright Law. Article 16 of the Copyright Law distinguishes different situations regarding the ownership of copyright in works made for hire. The court holds that the disputed work falls under the category of "special work made for hire" as specified in Item (2) of Paragraph 2 of Article 16, i.e., a work made for hire where "the copyright belongs to the legal person or other organization as stipulated by laws, administrative regulations, or agreed by contract." The reasons are as follows:

First, in this case, the parties indeed did not conclude a written contract regarding the ownership of the copyright in the disputed works. However, this was an action taken under specific historical conditions. As the judgment of the court of first instance stated, it would be difficult to require the parties in this case to have expressly agreed in advance, in accordance with the provisions of the Copyright Law, on the ownership of the copyright in a service work at the time of its creation. At the same time, because the laws and regulations in effect at that time also had no provisions on this issue, it is necessary to thoroughly examine the specific form adopted by the parties in their actions and their true expressions of intent, on the basis of which the ownership of the copyright in the disputed service work can be correctly determined.

Second, with regard to the legal environment at the time, China had not yet established a copyright legal system, and the general public lacked legal awareness of copyright protection, a fact which both parties to this case also acknowledged. Therefore, the situation described by witnesses occurred, where discussing rights was considered "a very dishonorable thing." This demonstrates that, with respect to the overall creation of animated films, the notion that the results of creation performed in the course of completing work tasks belonged to the unit was consistent with the general understanding of people at that time. In addition, during the production of the animated film *Calabash Brothers*, Jiang Youyi, then Director of the Creation Office of the Shanghai Animation Film Studio, explicitly instructed the creators not to submit their works for external publication, and the appellant in this case, as one of the creators, raised no objection to this requirement. The existing evidence also cannot prove that the appellant submitted the work to *Animation King* during the production period of *Calabash Brothers*. In other words, the appellant complied with the appellee's regulations through actual conduct. This fact indicates that both parties acknowledged that the appellee could impose the above requirements on the creators, including the appellant, meaning the appellee had the right to control and dispose of the character image designs of the animated film. Therefore, from the perspective of good faith, the appellant cannot later make a contrary expression of intent and claim authorship rights in the disputed character image artistic works.

Third, from the perspective of the appellee's conduct, the fact that the appellee did not interfere with the appellant's submission and publication of the *Calabash Brothers* comic book after the completion of the animated film does not indicate that the appellee waived its rights, but rather that it merely refrained from exercising its rights, specifically, from exploiting the economic benefits derived from the works. Because during this process, the appellee's copyright was not challenged, nor did any ownership dispute arise as in the present case, the appellee's conduct cannot be regarded as an expression of its position on the issue of ownership. Similarly, the fact that the appellee subsequently did not assert its rights as a plaintiff in related infringement lawsuits can only be understood in the same way, and not, as the appellant argues, as indicating that the appellee did not possess the status of a right holder.

Finally, in this case, the disputed "Calabash Brother" character image artistic works were indeed created by Hu Jinqing and Wu Yunchu and reflect their individual will. Therefore, the personality of the appellant as the author should be respected. Specifically, for such "special service works" as the disputed works, in accordance with the provisions of Article 16, paragraph 2 of the Copyright Law, the appellant shall enjoy the right of attribution, and all other copyright rights shall be enjoyed by the appellee.

In summary, the disputed "Calabash Brother" character image artistic works in this case are service works created by the appellant under specific historical conditions, and the appellee enjoys all copyright rights therein except the right of attribution. Therefore, the court of first instance correctly found the facts and correctly applied the law, and the appellant's grounds of appeal cannot be sustained. Accordingly, the Shanghai No. 2 Intermediate People's Court, in accordance with Article 153, paragraph 1, item (1) and Article 158 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, renders the following judgment on March 30, 2012:

The appeal is dismissed and the original judgment is affirmed.

This judgment is final.
